Hot and dry, and by these signs one shall know him: he is of pale color, as ash, and that signifies that the suction (heat) has consumed his moisture. He drinks more than he needs. In body he is lean and does not have much flesh; his face is thin and gaunt, and he is quick to anger, and anger stirs in him swiftly. He is steady in his works and is bold and quick in all his doings, and in his speech he has no measure. He is not fainthearted and has a proud heart, and is generous, and does not care to whom he gives. His worth lies in his heart, and his bones are coarse in him, and likewise his sinews. He is quick and brisk, and is not constant. He desires women gladly, and may perform much — thus one recognizes the choleric man.

The phlegmatic resembles water and winter, for he is cold and moist, and these are his signs: he is white in color and is fleshy and full of phlegm/mucus, because he has no heat. And he is stout, and vomits gladly [likely: urinates gladly]. He is fearful and not bold, and is not cheerful. He eats much and drinks little, and is sluggish in his affairs, and has soft hair, and does not desire many women, yet can perform much, because he is cold — and naturally all women are cold and moist. And therefore a wound-doctor who [treats] the wounds...

He shall also observe whether the person has a dry body and flesh, as a person around thirty years old, and also those who labor much and travel much, who are dry by nature in the body — to these he must give very drying remedies. And sometimes it happens that the moist nature is [actually] dry and the dry is moist; in this every physician must be very careful that he can proceed from one remedy to another according to what he observes in the person, so that he does not make the moist [person] dry, nor the dry moist, nor make the hot cold, nor the cold hot. Also some limbs of a person are of a much drier nature than others, such as the bones and the [sinews?], and therefore they need drier remedies than the others. And therefore a wise physician should be diligent, warming the wounds and making the flesh fresh in the wound, so that according to the nature and complexion of the person he makes the medicine, especially where the wounds do not want to heal. You should note that there are many kinds of wounds that afflict people, such as stabbed, hewn, struck, shot, or fallen (wounds); and in all other wounds a physician should be careful which are to be sutured — the suturing should be done skillfully and swiftly — and which are not to be sutured; of these he shall take heed according to his art. When the belly is wounded such that it becomes distended or swollen and inflamed, or [the wound extends] through the four [layers/regions?], it is a sign of death. Long stab-like wounds are all wounds in which there is not much flesh and much sinew, that is, wounds of the hands and of the bones and of the joints and of the sinew and of the tendons and of the veins, which are called lacerti [muscles/sinews], and four fingers above the knee and four downward, and by the ankle — if the bones become cut off or broken, this is all deadly and paralyzing, and sometimes deadly, so that the sickness in the wound turns back against the patient. He wishes to go and rest so that he cannot move, and great pain comes to him, and also cramp comes to the wound. In all wounds above the ill person and going forward, it is useful and good for the physician to make the patient a stool [purgative/laxative], so that the bad humors do not settle at the wound and multiply there. And in wounds which the sick person feels going downward again, the physician shall bring up and cause an evacuation from the stomach from above. And if it is a case where a coarse discharge of bone occurs, then heal only the wound and let the bone move; otherwise, if you want to heal the bone but not the wound, then the patient will be seized by spasm, that is, paralysis (Lemung).

Whether the blood be much or little, and all wounds of that kind require it.

The harmful wounds by cause [or 'concerning'] are such: all fresh wounds require only one strong pain-remedy together with a common medicine that belongs to it; and all fresh wounds require more drying medicine, and the small ones less. Hippocrates says that all wounds require drying medicine, except only the wounds of the belly, which should not be dried. In all deep, piercing, long or short wounds you shall be diligent that you join the lips of the wound well to one another, and if it needs stitching, then stitch it properly; and the deep ones you shall heal from the bottom up, so that no impurity or pus remains shut in within. Also note that all wounds that have healed but still are not sound within, these you must open again with a cut, so that the pus and impurity may flow out - how you should make the cut, that the size of the wound and its nature will teach you. You should know that there is no better medicine for all wounds than good wine. Warmed wine draws out the pus very effectively, as Hippocrates says, for wine renews and strengthens nature, and nature makes good flesh in the person, and good flesh brings good blood - for there is no greater cause in all wound-treatment than [this].

The drink shall be good old white wine, and moreover for whoever has a hard wound, the food and its regimen should follow its (the patient's) nature — that is the best medicine, and especially for women. Take terebinth (turpentine) and common oil and barley flour and boil that together. Every wound you shall first wash with warm wine-water, and dry the wound, make [a dressing] with a cloth.

Surgical apostles' ointment (Unguentum apostolicorum chirurgicum):
Take ship's pitch, one pound, pine resin, galbanum, serapinum, armoniacum, opoponax, each one ounce; wax, four ounces. Thus prepare it: the gum which one weighs may be pulverized; lay it in vinegar and let it dissolve in a pan over the fire — the galbanum, armoniacum, serapinum, opoponax and ship's pitch. And when they have dissolved, take a little of it and pour it into cold water; if it holds together like tallow, then it is good. After that, add powdered Greek pitch, mastic, and frankincense, each taken in equal amount, and stir it well through one another. And when it changes from the white color to the yellow color, then it is good. After that, take it off the fire and add turpentine to it, and stir it well through one another. Afterward pour it into a vessel and press it out well onto cold water. Afterward take it out of the water and make the hands wet with olive oil, and put it near the fire so that the water comes out of it.

I have seen many where the skin has not been cut, yet [the wound] is healed, and [I discuss] whereby the physician may recognize the wound, and only by warmth and warning. It also happens that the skull bone becomes cracked, so that it stands correctly, with only a small crack, so that one cannot recognize it well, and [that] the skull is neither lower nor higher than before. After that, take three loth of meal and mix it with the powder, and add thereto three loth of honey, and set it to the fire and stir it all together well until it becomes thick; and lay it warm on the swelling as long as it takes until the swelling opens up matter. And if the matter cannot come out, then make a hole in it so that the matter can flow out. Another [remedy] that also works: juice mixed with a fresh curd/cheese and laid warm upon the swelling.

Head [wound]: This is when the head is injured such that a part of the skull is knocked off but not shattered, and that same piece hangs down attached only by the skin. Then one should cut the skin in two places down to the knocked-off bone, and afterward loosen that piece of bone from the skin and throw it away. After that, fold the skin back up again and lift it at the top, and stitch it on both sides very skillfully and firmly with a silk needle, leaving the middle open where you have folded it back, so that you may heal the wound well. You should also note whether much skin hangs down from it; if so, you should cut all of it away together and throw it away, for otherwise it could not form a good scar (cicatrization).

If the throat is wounded with a sword or with a knife, the physician should first cleanse the wound very well and with his hand gently manipulate it. If there is anything lodged in the wound that should be removed — such as bone or some other debris — he should take it out from there. In the flow of the blood behind [the wound], he should stitch part of the wound closed and leave part open. And when the blood has been staunched, he should go in and remove from the wound whatever harmful matter remains inside, and then stitch it fully closed, yet leave it open at both edges because of the pus. Thereafter he should treat the wound as was taught before for other wounds.

But if the sinew (vessel) or the artery in the throat is wounded, so that the vessel protrudes out of the wound and blood spurts forth, then take a soft grown wool and lay it loosely at the edges. Afterward, cauterize it a little with a glowing iron, and then stitch the wound closed and proceed as was written before.

Manus (hand): if the hand is wounded, and thereby the sinews/veins and also the bone are cut through, then treat it as with other wounds of the arm. And if it is necessary, lay upon the hand a small compress so that the wound does not close together improperly, and further bind it and sprinkle red powder upon it, and proceed as before.

Venter (belly): concerning wounds of the belly, you should likewise note that the place on the body is soft to the touch. The skin of the belly is made of two layers, one on the outside which is coarse, and one beneath which is very soft, and is called amorita, according to which it truly has veins; and lacertoz, that is a hair-growth, which are full of sinews and very thin, just like a membrane, and are so joined together that they cannot be separated; and about this one holds that it is merely a skin of the belly and nothing more. After that there are two muscles (lacerti) which have flesh, which run down from the chest to the bone of the chest, and one is always joined to the other, and this is called myrat (?). And after that there is a small membrane which surrounds the whole belly, and it is called siphac (peritoneum), and it may bleed and is full of veins, and they join together from the right side.

results.translation: To the back, which has four [muscles / turns] and also the left side toward the back, and thereupon, near the skin of the belly on both sides, are two lacerti (muscles) which I have named before, and one goes down from the breast, and the other goes up from the breastbone; and near those lacerti are other lacerti which run along the length; and near that place the membrane called the peritoneum is grayish in color. And thereupon, if that place becomes wounded, it is always a dangerous wound reaching to the liver [and] the belly. If the middle of the belly is wounded, it is very hard to stitch, and it is very fearsome, because from the wound the intestines readily come out, and it is very hard afterward to put them back into the belly. And therefore, when the belly is wounded, the lacerti on both sides constrict so that the intestines must come out, because the belly itself has no lacerti (muscles) that could hold the intestines in. And therefore, where a narrow wound occurs in the belly [so] that the intestines come out, one must help very quickly before it swells and the cold causes it to swell up before the wound [heals], and if you cannot push it back in, then you should take a bath-sponge and soak it in warm wine and lay it upon the intestines.

Thus it lessens the swelling and the [inflammation?] disappears so that you can well remove it. This is the manner Galen teaches for such stitching: that one should begin at the [edge], at the skin, and stitch through the fat, and not through the membrane, and then go to the other part and stitch through it, continuing always outward until it is entirely stitched.

If it happens that the other intestines are wounded, then take a small tube of elder wood, as thick and as wide as the wounded intestine, and scrape it and make it thin enough to be handled with the fingers, and let the tube also be longer than the wound is. Afterward push the tube into the wounded intestine and let the tube extend well on both sides, and sew the wound together with a silk thread. Then clean the intestine of the excrement inside it entirely with a clean small pledget of lint soaked in warm wine, and when it is now quite clean, put it back in and stitch it so that it lies in its place, and lay it back. Afterward sew the wound of the belly as I have taught before, and do not let the wound of the belly remain open, as Master Rogerius and Rynald teach, for if the belly wound stood open, then the moisture could cause much harm and pain again, since air would enter, and the doctor would have much labor before he could heal the wound. And the other matter is that if discharge runs to the wound, the intestines might come out; therefore sew the wound and dry the moisture with good warm wine, and the bandage should always lie so that the wound is closed, and also take care that the moisture from the wounded intestine does not get onto anything else.

...again, and do as before, and thereafter leave the bandage on from the third day up to the third [day again], and give him the powder and the salve [pigment/ointment] that I taught before, and this you shall do to him every time for the wound. But if the wound is behind, in the chest, and no bowel comes out through it, then treat him as I taught before.

If the heart is wounded, then very black blood flows in great quantity from the wound. If the lung is wounded, then a foamy blood flows out of the wound. If the diaphragm — that is, the membrane of the chest — is wounded, then the patient has a great, labored breath and dies very quickly. If the liver is wounded, then clotted [curdled] blood flows out of it. If the stomach is wounded, then the food the patient has eaten comes out [through the wound], and such a wounded person is nearly always doomed — helpless, and no physician shall be able to heal or bind him. And as for the spleen, we commend that to God's care. It often happens that the lung is wounded such that it protrudes through the wound, and [if] the wound is [too] narrow, so that the lung cannot go back in, then you should not make the wound wider; rather see to it that the patient lies stretched out upon the ground [in a particular way, e.g. propped/inclined], as has been taught.

...an unskilled physician who does not have knowledge can, through his ignorance, [cause] many a sickness, and often death results from it, which need not happen if he were a good master and knew all the wounds in a person, how they are to be healed, as I have already taught above [concerning the hip and the treatment as with other wounds].

When the knee is so wounded that the kneecap is split, then bind the wound and fit the kneecap back as before; afterward wrap it as before, and remove all the [foreign matter/splinters] from the wound. The sinews above and below the knee are very dangerous, even deadly, if damaged, for there is nothing else there but sinews and veins. And where the bone is wounded, treat it just as with other wounds — with bandaging, with stitching, and with plumaceaux (lint dressings). And all wounds in the finger above the joint are deadly there too, and if the foot is so wounded, it is likewise [dangerous] there. And help in all such cases as is written above.

A general rule concerning wounds:
In all parts of the body, when it is wounded, you shall conduct and guide yourself according to the teaching given above. And where the wound of the head and of the face is, as written above — first you shall cleanse the wound of all filth, and if there is anything in the wound, such as bone or other things, that must come out, you shall remove it. Afterward, join the lips [edges] of the wound together.

A physician must for himself every day find new customs and teachings, and much equipment through which to recognize how the arrow should be removed; yet I will instruct you a little, and show you how you should master it. The shot arrow comes out of the wound in two ways: one, it comes out backward behind itself, or forward — that is, out again — and the arrow, when it goes out, must come out that way if it does not want to willingly go; then let it remain stuck in there until the flesh around the arrow decays, then it comes out easily on its own. And if it is stuck in the bone and will not come out, then let it remain stuck in for some days and move it a little every day often; and if it still will not come out, you must, with the tool ("negwer") made for this purpose, work it out around the shaft, and thus draw it out. And if that is the case, then take an instrument that is large enough to fill the socket of the arrow; then push the instrument into the socket of the arrow and press firmly, exactly as if you wanted [to push it] through the wounded bone, and thus draw it out very smoothly; or drive the iron into the flesh, then take pincers and draw it out very skillfully with them. But if a bolt ("pfrol") has been shot, then you should apply the bolt-remedy at each end of the bolt.

And his body should be such that he does not chew hard or coarse food, nor drink anything that harms, for as long as it takes until he is fully healed.

If the arm is shot through and the wound is not deadly, draw out the arrow, and wash both edges of the wound with prepared bacon fat, and proceed as described for the neck when shot through.

But if the arm is shot near a joint, then wash the same wound as before. If an arrow is shot into the breastbone or into the chest bone, then work the arrow-iron around it and thus draw it out. results.translation: There it is to be feared, when one wants to draw out the arrow, that it very easily happens that the iron remains in the stomach or in the belly; if the arrow shaft remains in it and one notices that it does not come out easily, it is very much to be feared that the person may die. Therefore the physician shall make a plaster from something that is soft, and make it mild, and lay the plaster on the place where you feel the point of the arrow, and on the plaster lay the thumbs around it, and press the arrow very swiftly so that it may draw back out again. Then the physician shall press the flesh/muscle very firmly together with his left hand near the shaft, and with his right hand he shall pull the shaft out very steadily with all effort, so that the iron does not remain in the stomach or the belly. And if the physician notices that he is pulling out the shaft but cannot get the iron out, he shall push the shaft back into the iron, and he who holds the thumb against the point of the arrow on the skin shall press very firmly so that the arrow-iron adheres well to the shaft; and thus, while the nail is pressed firmly with the thumb, the physician shall also press the flesh with his left hand near the wound of the shaft, and meanwhile he shall move the shaft and draw it out lengthwise.

results.translation: As often as in the arm the bones or another limb (or joint) is broken, the physician should be very skilled and should observe carefully in the fracture that the broken pieces of bone do not lie one upon another. When they lie on one another and the bone is broken, he should stretch the sinews and strengthen the muscle (flesh), and should with his hand handle and move the broken bone so as to bring it to fit, that the fracture stands correctly as if it were a whole bone. After that the physician should take blood from beneath the skin near the bone and smear it into the fracture and onto the bone, and afterward with honey. After that he should take the white of eight eggs or more and beat it in a bowl with a spoon until it foams well, and make of it a plaster on a cloth, as long as needed so that it can go around the bone at the fracture, and also as wide as needed so that it can well cover the fracture, so that it soaks into it well and makes it thoroughly wet with the egg white; afterward lay that upon the fracture and thereby treat the fracture, and take a bandage that is neither too long nor too wide, and wrap it fairly firmly so that the fracture may not be dislocated.

You should also know that dislocations of a limb are, some of them, heavier, some lighter; and after a dislocation of the sinews there comes a difficult setting, and after a dislocation of the fingers there comes an easy setting/joining. A light dislocation is that of the thumb and also of the shoulder, and this occurs in thin people and not in fat ones. A bad dislocation is that of the fingers, and often one must rather break them than dislocate them further. Also the elbow is bad, because it is difficult and hard to set back again. The middle kind of dislocation, which is neither heavy nor light, is that of the hip bone, and it requires a special setting of the joint-head. And the very worst dislocation is when the head of the dislocated bone is crushed or broken off, for then one can no longer set it and join it back to its natural place — as often happens at the head of the hip bone, and at the bone of the arm, and at the two shin bones below near [the ankle].

Let a fumigation of warm oil be applied. In case of a great tumor of the fatty tissue, if it is thick, let phlebotomy be performed [and] let it be purged afterward; the one who receives it should take... [and] apply to the neck something moist and let it be placed thereon. In cold [conditions] apply through the juice of lettuce and threads. If a tumor arose from the intestines, it teaches that: rue, applied warm, thus indeed helps as does parsley — [certain substance] and moist [remedy], without scalpel, these applied warm to a tumor of the belly which is like a priapism, tamed by moisture; and if the swelling does not diminish, phlebotomy [should be done]... and it requires a curative both compound and simple: apply doses of a poultice and water, and apply cold things to the thigh and leg, and anoint with some ointment. Then place chamomile and cut apples there. Wild agnus castus and rue are most useful, and further... this is a general cure of Master Hugo of the Danube, among the apostates of Verona, and those who did not know the authors — but perhaps he concealed it out of kindness and ease. Therefore I say in sum, drawn from above: a humor generated first by feeding, must be moderated by day and night so that it may flow more abundantly through the veins. A mallow leaf, and properly cooked, purges; apply it — let blood be drawn generously, but at the same time let the state be diminished, and apply without excess... apply where it is not yet seen to be enlarged; aim toward the expulsion of it, and use for this also leaves.

Drunk on an empty stomach once a day it cures the head's pain and swelling/tumor, is valuable against all fevers hot and cold, cleanses the sieve of the brain, restrains menstruation in those afflicted, purges the liver... and all fluxes of the belly, and purges the stomach well of bad humors.'
